source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: Scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs
finding: LLM-SR runs a generate-and-test loop. The LLM writes equation skeletons as Python, code fits the constants, scores go into an experience buffer, and the best items go back into the prompt. It beat symbolic-regression baselines on four problems, most clearly out of domain.
numbers: Table 1 NMSE. E. coli growth OOD: LLM-SR about 0.0037 (stated in text), baselines above 1 (PySR 1.4467 OOD). LLM-SR ran about 2.5K iterations, baselines over 2M. Setup: 4 skeletons per prompt, temperature 0.8, k=2 in-context examples.
limits: Table text is garbled by PDF extraction, so only the figures stated in prose are safe. Four small problems (two oscillators, E. coli growth, stress-strain).
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our loop. The model proposes, code fits and scores, and only real scores steer the next prompt (G2, G5). Held-out OOD data is the real test (G3).

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: Scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs (ablations)
finding: Each part of the loop matters. Removing the problem description, the program form, the refine loop, or the skeleton-plus-optimizer split all hurt.
numbers: w/o iterative refinement NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain, 1.81e-1 OOD. w/o skeleton+optimizer 3.78e-1 in-domain, 3.75e-1 OOD. w/o Prior (no natural-language description) gave a considerable drop; w/o Program a smaller one.
limits: GPT-3.5 backbone; the full-method NMSE for the same average was not restated in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Two-stage design: the model proposes structure, code fits numbers. Do not let the model emit final numeric values. Keep the domain description in the prompt.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: Scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs (memorisation check)
finding: Perplexity of Feynman equations under the LLM is much lower than for the authors' new problems. This points to recitation of known laws, not discovery.
numbers: Perplexity test with the Mixtral backbone; Feynman significantly lower. Stress-strain excluded (no ground-truth form).
quote: high likelihood of memorization of well-known Feynman equations by the LLM
limits: Indirect evidence. Low perplexity does not prove the solution was memorised.
agent_relevance: Any test of the agent on textbook laws is contaminated. Use altered or synthetic problems or it will look better than it is.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: a benchmark for scientific equation discovery with LLMs
finding: 239 problems in four domains. LSR-Transform rewrites known physical models into unusual forms; LSR-Synth makes synthetic problems. The best system reaches only about 31.5% symbolic accuracy.
numbers: Best symbolic accuracy 31.53% (LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini) on LSR-Transform; 31.5% is also the abstract's headline figure.
limits: Symbolic accuracy is judged against ground truth. The per-domain table was partly garbled in extraction, so I cite only the headline and the LSR-Transform column.
agent_relevance: Real discovery ability is far below what Feynman results suggest. Expect low exact-form recovery and lean on held-out checks.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: a benchmark for scientific equation discovery with LLMs (method comparison)
finding: Prompting without data does worst. Search loops with data feedback do much better. Backbone size is not the main driver.
numbers: LSR-Transform symbolic accuracy: direct prompting with no data, GPT-4o-mini 7.21%. LLM-SR: Llama-3.1-8B 30.63%, GPT-4o-mini 31.53%, GPT-3.5 10.81%. LaSR numeric accuracy (Acc0.1) 45.9 to 50.5% but symbolic accuracy only 5 to 13%.
limits: The paper guesses that smaller 'less opinionated' models explore better than GPT-3.5. That is a guess, not tested.
agent_relevance: Feedback from data is the main gain. Supports G2 and a data-first design.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: a benchmark for scientific equation discovery with LLMs (PySR and OOD)
finding: PySR matches or beats LLM methods on numeric fit but has near-zero symbolic accuracy outside physics. All methods get worse out of domain. Symbolic accuracy correlates with OOD accuracy.
numbers: PySR symbolic accuracy 0% on chemistry, biology and material science. ID-OOD gap larger in chemistry and biology than physics and material science. LSR-Transform harder than the original Feynman problems at the same tree size, even for 0 to 15 node equations.
limits: The correlation is across method-model-domain combinations, not independent trials.
agent_relevance: Fit alone does not prove a law (G3). The OOD gap is a signal code can count.

source: Grayeli et al. (2024) LaSR: Symbolic regression with a learned concept library
finding: LaSR adds a library of text concepts learned from the best hypotheses and calls an LLM only sometimes inside a genetic search. It solved more Feynman equations than PySR.
numbers: Exact solves of 100 Feynman equations: GPlearn 20, AFP 24, AFP-FE 26, DSR 23, uDSR 40, AI Feynman 38, PySR 59, LaSR 72 (GPT-3.5, LLM called 1% of steps). LaSR with Llama3-8B: 67, 69, 71 at 1%, 5%, 10% call rate.
limits: Feynman equations may be in training data; the authors test this separately (next line). One benchmark.
agent_relevance: A hybrid where code-run search owns the loop and the LLM is called rarely works. This is the model as proposer, not controller (G5).

source: Grayeli et al. (2024) LaSR (leakage control)
finding: On 41 synthetic equations built to look unlike textbook forms, LaSR still beat PySR, so the gain is not only recall.
numbers: Test-set R2: PySR 0.070, LaSR (Llama3-8B, LLM called 0.1% of steps) 0.913.
limits: R2 not exact match. 41 equations only. The authors say exact discovery is not the aim of this test.
agent_relevance: Add a leakage control (synthetic or altered problems) to every discovery test of our agent.

source: Grayeli et al. (2024) LaSR (call rate)
finding: Even a tiny LLM call rate with an 8B open model beats PySR.
numbers: Llama3-8B at 1% call rate: 67/100 exact solves versus PySR 59/100.
limits: I did not check wall-clock cost of the LLM calls.
agent_relevance: Small amounts of model guidance inside a programmatic search are a cheap lever.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: a coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
finding: An evolutionary loop over whole programs. An LLM ensemble proposes changes, automatic evaluators score them, a database keeps the best, and prompts evolve too. It extends FunSearch.
numbers: Over 50 open math problems: matched the best known on 75%, strictly improved on 20%. First rank-48 algorithm for 4x4 complex matrix multiplication (recursive Strassen gives 49); 14 matrix-multiplication targets improved; kissing number in 11 dimensions improved (593). Scheduling heuristic recovers 0.7% of fleet compute; kernel speedup 23% on average and 1% cut in Gemini training time.
limits: Needs a machine-checkable evaluator. The authors say many matched constructions are likely already optimal. Results are developer-reported; I found no independent replication of the whole set.
agent_relevance: Generate-and-test with a hard evaluator is the strongest result in this field. For us: code checks are the only judge (G5) and a database of earlier attempts goes into the prompt.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve (ablations)
finding: Ablations on tensor decomposition and kissing numbers remove evolution, prompt context, meta-prompt evolution, full-file evolution, or strong LLMs. The paper says AlphaEvolve does increasingly better as the underlying LLM improves.
numbers: Variants: No evolution (same start program fed repeatedly), No context in prompt, No meta prompt evolution, No full-file evolution, small LLM only. Effects shown in Fig. 8; the text gives no single number.
limits: Effect sizes are only in the figure, which I did not extract. Two tasks.
agent_relevance: An archive of earlier attempts and real problem context in the prompt are not decoration.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2024) Mathematical discoveries from program search with LLMs (FunSearch), Nature
finding: FunSearch pairs a code LLM with an automatic evaluator in an island-based evolutionary search over one function. Not opened this session (paywall redirect; PMC fetch returned HTML). AlphaEvolve's text confirms FunSearch evolves a single function only.
numbers: From memory, unverified here: cap set of size 512 in n=8 (previous best 496), plus better bin-packing heuristics.
limits: Numbers unverified. Treat as a lead only.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as AlphaEvolve; confirm numbers before citing.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: End-to-end agent: idea, code via Aider, experiments, paper, automated review. Cost under $15 per paper. Idea survival and implementation success vary strongly with the model.
numbers: One of three domain tables, Sonnet 3.5 / GPT-4o / DeepSeek Coder / Llama-3.1 405B: 51 ideas each; novel 49 / 41 / 42 / 31; experiments passed 38 / 17 / 32 / 21; completed papers 38 / 16 / 31 / 21; mean reviewer score 3.82 / 3.70 / 3.32 / 2.30 (scale 2 to 6); cost $250 / $300 / $10 / $120 (row-to-model mapping inferred from listed order).
limits: The reviewer is an LLM. Authors list failure modes: Aider fails to implement many ideas, wrong implementations are hard to catch, few experiments give 'deceptive or inaccurate conclusions', ideas repeat across runs.
agent_relevance: Implementation, not ideation, is the bottleneck. A real check of the code must stand between idea and claim (G2, G3).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist (reviewer validity)
finding: The automated reviewer is near human on ICLR data, but backbones differ in calibration. Sonnet 3.5 was over-optimistic and needed a stricter threshold.
numbers: Decision threshold at score 6 for most models, but 8 for Sonnet 3.5 to get calibrated results. Llama 3.1 405B struggled to follow the output format. Human-level AUC 0.65 reported.
limits: ICLR 2022 data may be in pre-training. Accepted papers are camera-ready, rejected ones original submissions, which may leak a style cue.
agent_relevance: LLM judges drift positive. Supports G5: no self-grading without a code check.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: workshop-level automated discovery via agentic tree search
finding: Replaces fixed code templates with best-first agentic tree search over code nodes and adds VLM feedback on figures. Three fully AI-written papers were submitted to an ICLR workshop.
numbers: One of three papers scored an average 6.33 (about the top 45%) and would have passed meta-review. That paper reported a negative result: a compositional regularisation term gave no significant gain and sometimes hurt.
limits: One of three; workshop level, not main track. Reviewers noted weak justification.
agent_relevance: Best-first tree search over attempts, with the real score as node value, is a concrete operator pattern (pick a node to debug or refine by score).

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: towards data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: Data-driven discovery tasks taken from real papers' workflows (DB-REAL) plus synthetic tasks (DB-SYNTH). The best agent scores only about 25%.
numbers: Best system 25% (hypothesis matching score). Best non-oracle score by domain: biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%. By workflow: correlation analysis 55%, data selection 18%, summary statistics 18%; spatial analysis, pollen dating, ecological modelling 0%. Hand replication took up to 90 person-hours per dataset and 30% failed.
limits: The results table was garbled by extraction. The paper's sentence on domain-knowledge hints reads 9.9% versus 17.5% in a confusing order, so I do not cite the direction.
agent_relevance: Data-first discovery on messy real data is far harder than clean equation fitting. Expect failure on spatial and advanced-statistics tasks.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench (scaffold comparison)
finding: Fancier reasoning scaffolds did not help a plain code-generation agent. Only oracle feedback (Reflexion with oracle) clearly helped.
numbers: Agents: CodeGen, ReAct, DataVoyager (planning with a self-critic), Reflexion (Oracle), NoDataGuess, on GPT-4o, GPT-4-0125 and Llama-3-70B. The paper says ReAct and self-critic planning 'do not help improve the simple CodeGen agent'. Almost all non-reflexion agents solve only the easiest instances.
quote: do not help improve the simple CodeGen agent
limits: A no-data baseline scoring near the agents suggests prior knowledge explains part of the score. Exact table cells not safely read.
agent_relevance: Support for G1 and G2: self-critique without a real signal adds nothing; real external signal adds the gain.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: a virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents
finding: 120 text-simulated discovery tasks across 8 topics and 3 difficulties. Human scientists do far better than three baseline agents (ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer).
numbers: Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge tasks. Humans (up to 11 per task): procedure 0.79, completion 0.66, knowledge 0.55; 11 of 16 tasks above 60% completion. Agents scored above 60% on unit-test sub-skills.
limits: Five seeds per task. Easy runs capped at 100 steps, others at 1000.
agent_relevance: Agents can do the pieces but fail the full hypothesise-test-conclude cycle. Explicit hypothesis memory (Hypothesizer) raised knowledge found but not completion.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld (brute force)
finding: Some solutions were brute force (for example trying all crystal frequencies) with no explanation of why, which the separate knowledge score catches.
numbers: Three scores per task: completion, process, explanatory knowledge. Completion can be high while knowledge is low.
limits: Qualitative remark in the discussion.
agent_relevance: Score the explanation separately from the outcome. An outcome check alone rewards brute force.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: 10 environments from psychology to ecology. Experiment choice is scored by expected information gain; discovery by whether an explanation helps another agent predict. All current models struggle.
numbers: Larger models (32B) beat 7B; closed beat open. GPT-4o has the lowest EIG regret. Box's Apprentice (LLM plus fitted statistical models) did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o and favoured overly simple forms such as linear fits for nonlinear systems.
limits: Per-environment scores are in figures. The Apprentice was omitted in two domains because GPT-4o could not use it reliably.
agent_relevance: Experiment choice can be scored by information gain in code (G5). Adding a model-fitting tool does not help automatically.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym (explanations)
finding: A novice agent reading the scientist's explanation predicts worse than the scientist who ran the experiments.
numbers: Explanations help in animal growth and struggle in complex domains such as moral judgement.
limits: The novice is also an LLM, so reader weakness and message loss are mixed.
agent_relevance: A written finding passed on loses information. Keep raw observations next to notes.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study
finding: Blind review by NLP experts: LLM ideas were judged more novel than 49 human experts' ideas, and slightly less feasible.
numbers: Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (p<0.05), AI plus human rerank 5.81. Excitement 4.55, 5.19, 5.46. Feasibility 6.61 human, 6.34 AI (not significant). 298 reviews from 79 reviewers. After LLM style normalisation expert judges told AI from human ideas at 50% accuracy.
limits: Ideas, not results. The authors say novelty judgment is hard even for experts and propose an execution study. Topics were controlled.
agent_relevance: Over-generate and rank gives novelty, but cheap ideas still need execution checks.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) (diversity and LLM judging)
finding: Over-generation collapses: of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 are non-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.8). LLMs are poor at absolute scores but fair at pairwise ranking.
numbers: Accepted-versus-rejected ICLR 2024 pairs (1200 submissions): Claude-3.5-Sonnet zero-shot 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%; no gain from few-shot or chain-of-thought.
limits: Duplicate threshold was set by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not independent (G4). Dedupe, then rank pairwise in code.

source: Ma et al. (2024) LLM and simulation as bilevel optimizers (Scientific Generative Agent)
finding: SGA splits the work. The LLM proposes discrete structure (an equation, a molecule); a differentiable simulator fits continuous parts and gives feedback. Tested on 4 constitutive-law and 4 molecule-design tasks.
numbers: 8 tasks: (a-d) constitutive law search, (e-h) molecule design. In the LLM-SRBench table SGA gets 9.91% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform with GPT-4o-mini (that table's number, not the SGA paper's).
limits: SGA's own headline numbers were not extracted. A simulator is required.
agent_relevance: Same split as LLM-SR: language model for structure, code for numbers and feedback.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Eureka: human-level reward design via coding LLMs
finding: Evolutionary search over reward code, 16 samples per iteration over 5 iterations, with 'reward reflection', a text summary of how each reward part behaved in training.
numbers: Beat human-written rewards on 83% of 29 tasks, mean normalised gain 52%. 16 samples were enough to get at least one runnable reward in the first round in every environment. A GPT-3.5 version degraded but still matched or beat humans on most Isaac tasks.
limits: Each evaluation needs RL training. The tasks postdate the GPT-4 knowledge cutoff, so contamination is unlikely.
agent_relevance: Text feedback built from measured numbers is a good revision input (G2). Sampling several and keeping the best by score is an operator.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: computational explorations of the creative process
finding: BACON and its successors (GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON, KEKADA) search a space of laws with a few data-driven heuristics, such as looking at the ratio of two variables that rise together. They rediscovered Kepler's third law, Ohm's law and Galileo's law, among others. Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers verified this session.
limits: BACON works on small, clean, preselected variables. LLM-SRBench and DiscoveryBench show messy data is still hard.
agent_relevance: These heuristics are the original operator library: ratio, product, linear fit, introduce an intermediate term. Our operators O1-O8 can be mapped to them and tested in an LLM-SR style loop.

source: King et al. (2009) The automation of science (Adam robot scientist)
finding: A closed-loop system formed hypotheses from a yeast metabolism model, chose and ran experiments on lab robots, and revised the model. Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers verified this session.
limits: Closed lab loop, domain-specific, not LLM-based.
agent_relevance: Closed-loop discipline: a hypothesis counts only after a test chosen to split competing hypotheses.

source: Cross-study reading by this agent (c01 to c27)
finding: In LLM-SR, LLM-SRBench, LaSR, AlphaEvolve, Eureka, DiscoveryBench and DiscoveryWorld, gains come when the model proposes and code scores and the real score feeds the next proposal. Scaffolds that added only model opinion (ReAct, self-critic) did not help.
numbers: No study read this session showed self-critique alone improving results; DiscoveryBench states the opposite directly.
limits: Reading by this agent; not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping G1, G2 and G5, and adding a code-scored archive of past attempts as prompt context.
